analysis.title: Build resilience as oil prices climb (UBS House View - Daily US)
key_insights: Brent crude hit USD 112/bbl for the first time since May and is on track for a third consecutive weekly gain. Brent is up 9.4% since the start of the month.

Fresh Middle East attacks raised supply concerns: Saudi Arabia reported attacks on an Aramco oil field and an airport in its Eastern Province, and the US ordered diplomats to leave the country amid Houthi strikes.
The New York Times reported that US and Israeli militaries have developed plans for renewed attacks on Iran after the US midterm elections on 3 November.
UBS says continuing geopolitical risks, including the Russia-Ukraine conflict, are likely to keep inflation concerns elevated and add to macro uncertainty.

UBS says resilient economic growth, robust corporate earnings and strong AI demand continue to underpin equity gains. It advises investors to focus on portfolio resilience to volatility rather than on short-term geopolitical drawdowns.
Since 1941, the S&P 500 has been higher 12 months after the start of a geopolitical crisis roughly three-quarters of the time.

OPEC crude production rose 0.92 million barrels per day in September to 25.1 million, about 85% of February's output. The G7 decision to release additional emergency oil stocks should give temporary relief.

UBS base case is that a gradual recovery of energy flows and production lets oil prices moderate into next year, so higher energy prices should not derail global growth. It acknowledges the physical oil market remains tight and vulnerable to further supply shocks.

UBS recommends broad commodities as a differentiated source of return and as a way to insulate portfolios from supply-driven volatility, citing power demand, AI infrastructure investment, electrification and constrained supply. It favors an actively managed approach.
UBS keeps a constructive equity outlook and recommends staying invested via broadly diversified exposure, adding fixed income, broad commodities and select alternatives for resilience.
Meta beat on revenue and earnings for the September quarter and raised the bottom of its 2026 capex range to USD 135-145bn from USD 130bn. Its shares rose 2.2% in post-market trading on Wednesday.

Meta's CEO said the company lacks sufficient compute capacity to expand its AI services globally. Meta also announced plans for a new class of non-voting stock, which could be used for capital fundraising.

UBS stays constructive on structural AI growth and recommends diversified exposure to companies with better earnings visibility. It suggests defensive areas of tech and rebalancing across sectors and regions for concentrated tech holders.

market_movers.rationale: Meta beat September-quarter revenue and earnings and raised the low end of its 2026 capex range to USD 135-145bn. Shares rose 2.2% after hours. UBS comments on AI demand generally and does not rate the company.

sector_views.rationale: UBS stays constructive on structural AI growth and favors companies with better earnings visibility, while suggesting defensive areas of tech and rebalancing for concentrated holders.

UBS suggests broad commodities as a differentiated return source and portfolio insulation against supply-driven volatility, citing power demand, AI infrastructure, electrification and constrained supply.

earnings_insights: Meta reported September-quarter revenue and earnings beats (the report gives no figures) and raised the bottom of its 2026 capex outlook to USD 135-145bn from USD 130bn.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Highest since May, up 9.4% since the start of October, third straight weekly gain. Keeps inflation concerns elevated.

macro_indicators.reading: 25.1 million bpd, up 0.92 million bpd in September, about 85% of February output
macro_indicators.interpretation: Supply is recovering but is still below pre-war levels.
UBS base case is that a gradual recovery in energy flows lets oil prices ease, leaving the growth impact insufficient to derail the economy.

trade_ideas.description: Add broad commodities and energy exposure to diversified portfolios as a hedge against supply-driven volatility
trade_ideas.rationale: Low correlations with traditional asset classes and an upcycle supported by power demand, AI infrastructure, electrification and constrained supply.

risk_factors: Further Middle East supply disruptions while the physical oil market remains tight.
Elevated inflation concerns from persistent geopolitical risk.
Possible renewed US/Israeli strikes on Iran after the 3 November midterms.
Concentrated tech positions that could suffer if market strength reverses.
vol_and_positioning: UBS advises positioning for periods of volatility through diversification, fixed income, broad commodities and select alternatives, rather than reacting to short-term geopolitical drawdowns.
geopolitical: Attacks on an Aramco oil field and an airport in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province.
The US ordered diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi strikes.
The New York Times reported US and Israeli plans for renewed attacks on Iran after the US midterm elections on 3 November.
The G7 decided to release additional emergency oil stocks.

tension_points.bull_case: OPEC output is recovering toward about 85% of February levels, trade routes are shifting and the G7 is releasing emergency stocks. UBS expects oil to moderate into next year without derailing growth.
tension_points.bear_case: The physical oil market remains tight and exposed to further supply shocks. Fresh attacks in Saudi Arabia and possible renewed strikes on Iran keep inflation concerns elevated.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Further supply shocks, such as renewed US/Israeli attacks on Iran after the 3 November midterms, would undermine the moderation view.
